Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens:
Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement
for Agentic Systems

Xin Xu    Ke Cheng    Hao Wang    Yangru Huang    Yanghao Xiao    Zhichao Chen    Zhisheng Zhong    Xun Liu    Yi Li    Qian Li    Haibin Lv    Jun Zhang    Jie Jiang    Zhouchen Lin
Abstract

Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version often exhausts the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. Inspired by the draft–verify principle of speculative decoding, we propose Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), a two-level framework coupling inner-loop agent search with outer-loop improver learning. SpecRSI drafts successors before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while adopting only fully evaluated, admissible versions. In the inner loop, Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. In the outer loop, Group Verification Optimization (GVO) updates the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. We evaluate SpecRSI on scientific optimization (including active queue management (AQM) for network infrastructure), coding, and general agent-system benchmarks. Under matched evaluation-call budgets, SpecRSI improves scientific terminal gain over Janus by 60.0%–96.3% and area under the budget curve by 32.1%–91.6%, while achieving higher means across all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs and outperforming MetaRSI-v1 by 1.30–2.70 percentage points (pp) in system score across twenty backbones. On instance-level comparisons, it further improves PyBaMM terminal gain by 142.6% and SWE-Pro success by 6.0 pp at 7.0% and 9.2% lower token cost, respectively. These results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

1 Introduction

Agent systems can improve through successive revisions to their prompts, tools, and workflows, and recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this goal to the mechanisms that generate subsequent improvements. Recent systems revise agent programs (Zhang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026b), modify the meta-agent that proposes revisions (Zhang et al., 2026b), adapt improvement operators and their scheduling in MetaRSI (Tan et al., 2026), or co-evolve target programs and proxy evaluators to allocate expensive real evaluations in Janus (Liu et al., 2026). Across these approaches, proposing changes and establishing their benefits both consume time and computation. This allocation problem is central to Web infrastructure and agentic systems: in active queue management (AQM), revising a controller to manage queue buildup and delay requires assessing traffic delivery, delay, loss, and fairness across diverse scenarios, consuming substantial simulator resources (Liu et al., 2026; de Almeida et al., 2024). This raises a central question: how should an agent allocate its limited budget between exploring new revisions and verifying their benefits? Useful revisions often support later improvements, yet identifying them requires expensive evaluation; the challenge is turning exploration into verified progress before resources run out (Figure 1).

Two limiting strategies expose this trade-off. Following one fully evaluated lineage gives every decision fresh feedback, but narrows the alternatives and places an evaluation barrier between dependent edits—for instance, when a coding-agent revision adds a file–test map that a successor uses for focused intermediate retesting while retaining the final full suite. Maintaining many lineages explores more broadly, but fully evaluating them all spends budget on branches that are never used. Extra workers cut elapsed time without making evaluation free, and under a fixed budget a wider search may not leave enough computation to finish the most useful branch. While prior systems partially relax this barrier by separating expansion from evaluation or validating in parallel (Wang et al., 2026b; Hu et al., 2026), we focus on drafting successors ahead of their parents’ full evaluation and jointly selecting further revisions and bundles of outstanding checks under the remaining budget.

Allowing successors to be drafted ahead changes where the budget should be spent next. A candidate that looks strong may still need several checks before it can be adopted, whereas a child that repairs an unhelpful parent may need only one remaining check. Evaluating a version solely by its apparent quality misses the cost of making it usable. Under a hard budget, what matters is a continuation—a sequence of further edits and checks from the current state—and the verified improvement it can still deliver with the remaining budget. Because this return must be estimated before paying for the checks that reveal it, scoring must shift from static candidate quality to the marginal verified return of further editing and checking.

Extending speculation from tokens to agent revisions therefore changes the search space, the verification process, and the learning objective. Agent versions are revisable programs whose successors may repair or build on a parent that is not yet admissible. Verification requires paid, complementary external checks with heterogeneous costs and dependencies; several may be jointly necessary for adoption, so a single target-model pass cannot supply this evidence. Progress must consequently be measured by realized verified gains under resource limits, accounting for all incurred search costs, including failed and unfinished work.

Contributions. We introduce SpecRSI, a framework for budgeted speculative agent improvement.  Two-Level Speculative Self-Improvement. We decouple speculative exploration from verified adoption: inner searches extend incompletely evaluated versions but adopt only fully evaluated, admissible ones, while the improver remains frozen within each search and learns from complete-search feedback between rounds.  Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS). VATS allocates the remaining budget across drafting and verification: the Solver preserves affordable completion bundles, including individually low-value checks; the Scorer predicts verified gains attainable through further edits and checks within the remaining budget; and the Policy selects the next draft or verification plan.  Group Verification Optimization (GVO). GVO assigns credit across independent complete searches from the same start, using verified gains from searches under matched resource caps to provide delayed credit to sampled edits and work choices for the Drafter and Policy, while training the Scorer on realized suffix returns and paid same-state comparisons.

2 Preliminaries and Related Work

2.1 Speculative Decoding

Speculative decoding uses a cheap draft model qq to propose tokens ahead of a target model pp (Leviathan et al., 2023). Given prefix x<ix_{<i}, let qi=q(⋅∣x<i)q_{i}=q(\cdot\mid x_{<i}) and pi=p(⋅∣x<i)p_{i}=p(\cdot\mid x_{<i}):

xi∼qi,αi=min⁡{1,pi​(xi)qi​(xi)},x_{i}\sim q_{i},\qquad\alpha_{i}=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{p_{i}(x_{i})}{q_{i}(x_{i})}\right\}, (1)

where ii indexes the token position, xix_{i} is the sampled draft token, and αi\alpha_{i} is its acceptance probability. Evaluating a draft block in parallel, the target model retains the accepted prefix; at the first rejection, it samples a replacement token from the normalized positive part of pi−qip_{i}-q_{i} and discards the remaining drafts, preserving the target distribution. SpecRSI brings this draft–verify separation to agent revisions (Figure 1), where acceptance requires complete admissible evidence instead of token-distribution equivalence (extended related work is in Appendix A).

2.2 Recursive Self-Improvement

In recursive self-improvement (RSI), we distinguish an agent version cc—comprising executable code and persistent prompts, tools, and workflows—from an improver Θ\Theta that proposes and selects revisions; updating Θ\Theta changes how subsequent rounds generate improvements. Given retained versions 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} and observed history HtH_{t}, a proposal–evaluation step within round kk is

c~t∼ProposeΘk(⋅∣𝒱t,Ht),zt=freal(c~t),(𝒱t+1,Ht+1)=Update⁡(𝒱t,Ht,c~t,zt),\begin{gathered}\widetilde{c}_{t}\sim\operatorname{Propose}_{\Theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{V}_{t},H_{t}),\quad z_{t}=f_{\rm real}(\widetilde{c}_{t}),\\ (\mathcal{V}_{t+1},H_{t+1})=\operatorname{Update}(\mathcal{V}_{t},H_{t},\widetilde{c}_{t},z_{t}),\end{gathered} (2)

where tt indexes steps under fixed Θk\Theta_{k}, c~t\widetilde{c}_{t} is the proposed version, and ztz_{t} is its evaluation outcome. A full real evaluation returns freal​(c)=(J⁡(c),v⁡(c))f_{\rm real}(c)=(J(c),v(c)), with utility J⁡(c)J(c) (higher is better) and admissibility indicator v⁡(c)∈{0,1}v(c)\in\{0,1\}. Based on ztz_{t}, Update\operatorname{Update} revises 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} and HtH_{t}; retained stepping stones need not immediately outperform the incumbent.

3 Method

3.1 Motivation

Accurate benefit evaluation is central to guiding RSI toward better agents under a limited search budget. If benefit evaluation is inaccurate, search either overlooks useful multi-step edits or wastes resources on candidates that never become admissible. Effective allocation must therefore evaluate the verified improvement that continued work can deliver.

Estimating this benefit is non-trivial because a candidate’s current quality does not determine the value of continuing from it, due to two challenges.  Benefit evaluation should reflect downstream verified improvement. Intermediate revisions may serve as stepping stones to later gains, but realizing those gains requires subsequent edits and real checks.  Benefit evaluation should account for completion costs. Complementary checks, planning, and failed attempts all draw from the same finite resources, so even promising gains may be too costly to verify. Together, these challenges induce a performance–cost trade-off: a worthwhile continuation must offer sufficient verified improvement while remaining affordable to complete. Figure 2 illustrates this trade-off across ten backbones, and Section 4.5 analyzes broader lifecycle expenditure.

3.2 Two-level Speculative RSI Loop

SpecRSI brings the draft–verify separation of speculative decoding to the RSI loop, allowing successor agent versions to be drafted before their parents are fully evaluated while allocating real checks selectively. Unlike token acceptance in Equation (1), adopting an agent requires complete admissible evidence. Specifically, we refine Equation (2) by organizing retained versions 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} as nodes in a search tree 𝒯=(𝒞,𝒜)\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A}) anchored at a complete admissible root rr, where 𝒞\mathcal{C} stores immutable agent versions and 𝒜\mathcal{A} records executed edit edges, and by decomposing frealf_{\rm real} into paid checks. Each version freezes its prompts, tools, workflows, and permitted persistent state (including memory), with model-parameter edits allowed only under D/H/M permissions. An uneditable verification contract Γ\Gamma specifies a finite required-item set ℐ\mathcal{I}, execution and admission rules, and constraints; its score JΓJ_{\Gamma} and admissibility condition instantiate the utility JJ and indicator vv from Section 2.2. At any step, state S=(𝒯,ℰ,H,B,N,nwrk)S=(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},H,B,N,n_{\mathrm{wrk}}) tracks admitted evidence ℰ\mathcal{E}, history HH, remaining expense budget B≥0B\geq 0, remaining attempts N≥0N\geq 0, and worker count nwrk≥1n_{\mathrm{wrk}}\geq 1. In token-accounted runs, BB and expense charges are measured in k tokens under the registered cap (while end-to-end totals also include overhead outside that cap), and elapsed time is tracked separately. For version cc and item ii, mc​i∈{0,1}m_{ci}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether a valid outcome is present, regardless of whether it passed. The complete admissible set and its best observed gain are

𝒞full(S)={c∈𝒞:mc​i=1∀i∈ℐ,c admissible},F⁡(S)=maxc∈𝒞full​(S)⁡[JΓ​(c)−JΓ​(r)],\begin{gathered}\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{full}}(S)=\{c\in\mathcal{C}:m_{ci}=1\ \forall i\in\mathcal{I},\ c\text{ admissible}\},\\ F(S)=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{full}}(S)}[J_{\Gamma}(c)-J_{\Gamma}(r)],\end{gathered} (3)

where admissibility is judged under Γ\Gamma and F⁡(S)F(S) is the observed adoption-ready gain rather than a learned estimate; because root rr is eligible, search-time F⁡(S)≥0F(S)\geq 0, while held-out gain is evaluated separately. The fixed contract Γ\Gamma and execution interface AcquireΓ\operatorname{Acquire}_{\Gamma} constitute the real evaluator: Γ\Gamma defines valid evidence, VERIFY invokes AcquireΓ\operatorname{Acquire}_{\Gamma} to run selected real checks, and complete admissible evidence determines JΓ​(c)J_{\Gamma}(c) and ACCEPT eligibility. By contrast, the learned Scorer Q^ϕ​(S,ω)\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,\omega) for proposed work ω\omega serves as the score evaluator, predicting continuation gain with optional expense and elapsed-time penalties (Equation (6)) to guide budget allocation without supplying evidence, whereas DRAFT generates successor edits without assigning evaluation scores.

At outer round kk, a complete admissible agent ckc_{k} serves as root rr. SpecRSI parameterizes the improver as Θk=(θk,ψk,ϕk,ν)\Theta_{k}=(\theta_{k},\psi_{k},\phi_{k},\nu), comprising Drafter parameters θk\theta_{k}, work-selection Policy parameters ψk\psi_{k}, continuation-value Scorer parameters ϕk\phi_{k}, and fixed menu settings ν\nu. During search collection, all four components are frozen, with scorer snapshot ϕ¯k=ϕk\bar{\phi}_{k}=\phi_{k}. After G≥2G\geq 2 independent inner searches (counting distinct search runs rather than shared-tree leaves), GVO updates the learned parameters:

Inner loop:(ck+1(g),𝒟k(g))=SearchΘk(ck),g=1,…,G,Outer loop:𝒟k=⋃g=1G𝒟k(g),Θk+1=GVO(Θk,𝒟k),\begin{gathered}\text{Inner loop:}\kern 5.0pt(c_{k+1}^{(g)},\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(g)})=\operatorname{Search}_{\Theta_{k}}(c_{k}),\quad g=1,\ldots,G,\\[2.0pt] \text{Outer loop:}\kern 5.0pt\mathcal{D}_{k}=\bigcup\nolimits_{g=1}^{G}\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(g)},\quad\Theta_{k+1}=\operatorname{GVO}(\Theta_{k},\mathcal{D}_{k}),\end{gathered} (4)

where gg indexes the GG searches, each Search\operatorname{Search} returns an admissible successor ck+1(g)c_{k+1}^{(g)} and trajectory log 𝒟k(g)\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(g)}, and GVO updates (θ,ψ,ϕ)(\theta,\psi,\phi) from their union 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} while keeping ν\nu, Γ\Gamma, and the outer update rule fixed (Figure 3; see Algorithm S1 and Algs. S2–S3 in Appendix D). Across outer rounds, Reset returns the task root to c0c_{0}, whereas Carry retains a complete admissible successor chosen by the registered inter-round selector; both choices operate independently of within-search acceptance and GVO updates, and neither resets the learned improver.

Whereas Janus co-evolves programs with proxy evaluators (Liu et al., 2026) and MetaRSI learns operator schedules (Tan et al., 2026), SpecRSI learns to allocate budget between drafting and verification from complete-search verified returns (Appendix A).

3.3 Inner-loop Search with VATS

Within each inner search, Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) iteratively selects bounded work ω\omega under expense and attempt caps: either DRAFT​(P,h)\textsc{DRAFT}(P,h), where P=(Pa)a=1|P|P=(P_{a})_{a=1}^{|P|} indexes existing parent versions and h≥1h\geq 1 bounds edit depth, or VERIFY​(𝒥)\textsc{VERIFY}(\mathcal{J}), where 𝒥\mathcal{J} specifies verification jobs on existing versions. Either action may repeat until ACCEPT terminates the search. Because complementary checks cannot be scheduled by token-confidence ranking alone, VATS coordinates three modules under the frozen improver: the Solver constructs feasible completion bundles, the Scorer refines verification scope, and the Policy selects the next action before execution updates the state for replanning (Appendix D).

3.3.1 Solver

The Solver assembles completion bundles that fit within the remaining budget. For version cc, let Uc​(S)={i∈ℐ:mc​i=0}U_{c}(S)=\{i\in\mathcal{I}:m_{ci}=0\} denote missing items and Kc​(S)={(c,i):i∈Uc​(S)}K_{c}(S)=\{(c,i):i\in U_{c}(S)\} the corresponding outstanding outcomes. A relation reader ℛ⁡(S)=Remaining⁡(S)\mathcal{R}(S)=\operatorname{Remaining}(S) extracts masks, dependencies, shared setups, and source relations from existing records without running new checks or substituting forecasts for missing evidence (Appendix D). To ensure that versions can reach full admissibility even when individual checks carry little standalone value, the Solver forms bundled options:

Ωt=𝒟draft,t∪{VERIFY​(A):A∈ℳt}∪{ACCEPT},\Omega_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\rm draft,t}\cup\{\textsc{VERIFY}(A):A\in\mathcal{M}_{t}\}\cup\{\textsc{ACCEPT}\}, (5)

where Ωt\Omega_{t} is the feasible work menu at decision tt, 𝒟draft,t\mathcal{D}_{\rm draft,t} contains retained draft plans (which may extend incomplete parents), and ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} contains feasible verification bundles AA. Specifically, a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) selects bundles covering target KcK_{c} sets and cross-branch unions subject to prerequisites, shared setups, conflicts, and reserved budgets. While feasibility guarantees neither passing check outcomes nor exhaustive tree coverage, original completion seeds remain eligible throughout subsequent refinement.

3.3.2 Scorer

The Scorer Q^ϕ​(S,ω)\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,\omega) estimates the continuation value of state–work pairs under the frozen procedure π\pi (which encompasses edit generation and work selection under fixed menu rules), accounting for subsequent edits, checks, and branch switches:

Qπ(St,ω)=𝔼π[F(Send)−F(St)−λCt:end−μLt:end∣St,ω],Q^{\pi}(S_{t},\omega)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\bigl[F(S_{\rm end})-F(S_{t})-\lambda C_{t:{\rm end}}-\mu L_{t:{\rm end}}\mid S_{t},\omega\bigr], (6)

where StS_{t} is the state after settling the current preparation cost from pre-preparation state St−S_{t}^{-} (Alg. S2), and SendS_{\rm end} is the terminal state. Subsequent expense Ct:endC_{t:{\rm end}} and elapsed time Lt:endL_{t:{\rm end}} include later preparation and failed work but exclude sunk preparation at step tt. Fixed weights λ,μ≥0\lambda,\mu\geq 0 convert expense and elapsed time into score-unit penalties (μ=0\mu=0 in cost-only settings; our reference profile sets λ=μ=0\lambda=\mu=0, relying on resource inputs and hard caps rather than explicit return penalties). By definition, Qπ​(S,ACCEPT)=0Q^{\pi}(S,\textsc{ACCEPT})=0, and Scorer predictions never replace observed FF or admitted evidence.

Given a feasible bundle AA, let DjD_{j} denote job jj together with its prerequisites. The frozen scorer snapshot Q^ϕ¯\widehat{Q}_{\bar{\phi}} refines AA by evaluating the marginal gain of adding DjD_{j}:

Δϕ¯​(j∣A,S~)=Q^ϕ¯​(S~,VERIFY​(A∪Dj))−Q^ϕ¯​(S~,VERIFY​(A)),\Delta_{\bar{\phi}}(j\mid A,\widetilde{S})=\widehat{Q}_{\bar{\phi}}(\widetilde{S},\textsc{VERIFY}(A\cup D_{j}))-\widehat{Q}_{\bar{\phi}}(\widetilde{S},\textsc{VERIFY}(A)), (7)

where both terms are evaluated at the same conservative state S~\widetilde{S} that reserves the preparation cap. Comparing whole bundles captures cross-check interactions without summing isolated check scores, counting shared jobs and setups only once. Query and extension caps bound refinement overhead while preserving the eligibility of initial feasible seeds (Appendix D).

3.3.3 Policy

Once preparation cost is settled, the Policy selects work from the nonempty menu Ωt\Omega_{t} conditioned on observed relations ℛt=Remaining⁡(St)\mathcal{R}_{t}=\operatorname{Remaining}(S_{t}). With temperature-scaled logits ζt​(v)=zψ​(St,ℛt,v)/Tpol\zeta_{t}(v)=z_{\psi}(S_{t},\mathcal{R}_{t},v)/T_{\rm pol}, the sampling distribution is

πψ​(ω∣St,ℛt,Ωt)=(1−ϵ)​exp⁡(ζt​(ω))∑v∈Ωtexp⁡(ζt​(v))+ϵ|Ωt|,\pi_{\psi}(\omega\mid S_{t},\mathcal{R}_{t},\Omega_{t})=(1-\epsilon)\frac{\exp(\zeta_{t}(\omega))}{\sum_{v\in\Omega_{t}}\exp(\zeta_{t}(v))}+\frac{\epsilon}{|\Omega_{t}|}, (8)

where v∈Ωtv\in\Omega_{t}, Tpol>0T_{\rm pol}>0 is the sampling temperature, and ϵ∈[0,1)\epsilon\in[0,1) is the uniform-exploration rate. Because preference logits zψz_{\psi} are parameterized separately from value estimates Q^\widehat{Q} (with the ACCEPT logit fixed to zero), the Policy need not greedily maximize Q^\widehat{Q}. Search collection samples from πψ\pi_{\psi}, whereas deployment selects the maximum-logit action (Appendix D).

3.3.4 Execution and Acceptance

DRAFT. Given draft plan (P,h)(P,h), the Drafter initializes ca,0=Pac_{a,0}=P_{a} for each parent a=1,…,|P|a=1,\ldots,|P| and sequentially generates edits up to depth d=1,…,hd=1,\ldots,h using only the context Ha,dH_{a,d} observed prior to that edit:

ea,d∼πθ(⋅∣ca,d−1,Ha,d),ca,d=Freeze(Apply(ca,d−1,ea,d)),e_{a,d}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c_{a,d-1},H_{a,d}),\quad c_{a,d}=\operatorname{Freeze}(\operatorname{Apply}(c_{a,d-1},e_{a,d})), (9)

where ea,de_{a,d} is sampled from πθ\pi_{\theta}, Apply\operatorname{Apply} executes the edit, and Freeze\operatorname{Freeze} stores the resulting immutable version ca,dc_{a,d}. The executor Generateθ⁡(P,h,S)\operatorname{Generate}_{\theta}(P,h,S) runs this bounded plan on actual artifacts: incomplete parents may be extended, provided each edit waits for its immediate parent. Any invalid edit is charged to the budget and terminates that path while preserving its valid prefix.

VERIFY. For requested jobs Jobs⁡(ω)\operatorname{Jobs}(\omega), AcquireΓ\operatorname{Acquire}_{\Gamma} either retrieves valid identical records or executes real checks. Our core configuration runs direct checks only, whereas checked reuse imports results after scoped equality checks via the shared backend used by compatible controls. The executor records outcomes and updates the state before VATS replans (Appendix D).

ACCEPT. Admitted records must satisfy identity, scope, field, and provenance requirements, including for failed checks. Upon termination, VATS adopts

ACCEPT​(S)∈arg​maxc∈𝒞full​(S)⁡JΓ​(c),\text{ACCEPT}(S)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{full}}(S)}J_{\Gamma}(c), (10)

returning the root rr if it attains the maximum, and otherwise the first maximizer under a fixed version order. Only the adopted version requires complete admissible evidence, and the reference rule introduces no hidden completion or adoption margin.

3.4 Outer-loop Learning with GVO

Outer-loop training begins with supervised warm-up and then alternates between frozen-improver search collection and Group Verification Optimization (GVO) updates. Completed trajectories provide two supervision signals derived strictly from observed outcomes under the frozen improver rather than updated Scorer predictions: realized suffix returns train the Scorer (when return or pair records are present), and whole-search advantages train the Drafter and Policy over sampled choices (with empty empirical loss terms contributing zero).

3.4.1 Supervised Warm-up

Prior to the first collection round, supervised warm-up initializes Θ0\Theta_{0} by training Drafter θ\theta to imitate executed legal edits, Policy ψ\psi to imitate legal plan choices, and Scorer ϕ\phi to predict observed returns; unexecuted alternatives receive no labels. Throughout training, Solver feasibility rules and menu settings ν\nu remain fixed, and neither Solver outputs nor environment outcomes carry policy likelihoods.

3.4.2 Search Returns and Advantages

In each round, we run G≥2G\geq 2 independent searches from a shared pre-preparation state S0−S_{0}^{-} under frozen Θk\Theta_{k}, matching the root agent, verification contract, budgets, and worker count. Each search gg terminates at state SendgS_{\rm end}^{g} without requiring every visited version to be fully evaluated, logging total expense CgC_{g} and elapsed time LgL_{g} (including initial preparation as well as failed or unfinished work):

Rg=F⁡(Sendg)−F⁡(S0−)−λ​Cg−μ​Lg,Ag=Rg−1G−1​∑u=1,u≠gGRu,\begin{gathered}R_{g}=F(S_{\rm end}^{g})-F(S_{0}^{-})-\lambda C_{g}-\mu L_{g},\\ A_{g}=R_{g}-\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{u=1,\,u\neq g}^{G}R_{u},\end{gathered} (11)

where RgR_{g} is the net return of search gg and AgA_{g} is its leave-one-out advantage across the group {1,…,G}\{1,\ldots,G\}. Here F⁡(S)F(S) is the best observed complete admissible gain over root rr (Equation (3)), while λ​Cg\lambda C_{g} and μ​Lg\mu L_{g} penalize total cost and time in score units; if a search yields no new complete improvement, its gain is zero while incurred costs are still charged. Comparing whole searches eliminates the need for a learned baseline and assigns delayed credit to intermediate edits through their verified descendants, even when those intermediate versions are not themselves admissible.

3.4.3 Scorer Training

The Scorer is updated by minimizing a combined regression and pairwise objective, minϕ⁡[ℒQ​(ϕ)+βpair​ℒpair​(ϕ)]\min_{\phi}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\phi)+\beta_{\rm pair}\mathcal{L}_{\rm pair}(\phi)\bigr] with weight βpair≥0\beta_{\rm pair}\geq 0. The regression loss ℒQ\mathcal{L}_{Q} fits realized, undiscounted suffix returns from executed plan starts:

Gt=F(Send)−F(St)−λCt:end−μLt:end,ℒQ​(ϕ)=𝔼(St,ωt,Gt)∼𝒟Q​[(Q^ϕ​(St,ωt)−Gt)2],\begin{gathered}G_{t}=F(S_{\rm end})-F(S_{t})-\lambda C_{t:{\rm end}}-\mu L_{t:{\rm end}},\\ \mathcal{L}_{Q}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(S_{t},\omega_{t},G_{t})\sim\mathcal{D}_{Q}}\big[(\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S_{t},\omega_{t})-G_{t})^{2}\big],\end{gathered} (12)

where GtG_{t} is the realized net return from executing ωt\omega_{t} at paid state StS_{t}, and 𝒟Q\mathcal{D}_{Q} collects the resulting state–work–return triples under the frozen procedure (including paid alternatives). Here F⁡(Send)−F⁡(St)F(S_{\rm end})-F(S_{t}) is the remaining observed gain, and Ct:end,Lt:endC_{t:{\rm end}},L_{t:{\rm end}} measure expense and elapsed time from step tt to termination; unlike RgR_{g}, GtG_{t} excludes sunk preparation at step tt while charging subsequent preparation, so Q^ϕ\widehat{Q}_{\phi} estimates the conditional expectation QπQ^{\pi} via mean squared error.

To sharpen relative comparisons between legal plans a,ba,b at the same saved paid state SS, paid rollouts under the shared continuation policy estimate mean returns G¯a,G¯b\overline{G}_{a},\overline{G}_{b} and their difference δ^a​b=G¯a−G¯b\widehat{\delta}_{ab}=\overline{G}_{a}-\overline{G}_{b}:

ℒpair​(ϕ)=𝔼𝒟pair​[(Q^ϕ​(S,a)−Q^ϕ​(S,b)−δ^a​b)2],\mathcal{L}_{\rm pair}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm pair}}\bigl[(\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,a)-\widehat{Q}_{\phi}(S,b)-\widehat{\delta}_{ab})^{2}\bigr], (13)

where 𝒟pair\mathcal{D}_{\rm pair} stores matched tuples (S,a,b,δ^a​b)(S,a,b,\widehat{\delta}_{ab}). While ℒQ\mathcal{L}_{Q} anchors absolute value levels (which pairwise differences alone cannot identify), ℒpair\mathcal{L}_{\rm pair} directly supervises relative plan rankings. Generating these pairs restores paid state SS, forces a legal initial plan, and continues under the frozen improver; the resulting rollouts train only the Scorer, with all clones and rollouts charged to the budget and logged failures retained as valid data (whereas missing records are never imputed as zero).

3.4.4 Drafter and Policy Training

The actor parameters ϑ=(θ,ψ)\vartheta=(\theta,\psi) are updated over sampled edit tokens and plan choices via minϑ⁡[ℒGVO​(ϑ)+βKL​ℒKL​(ϑ)]\min_{\vartheta}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\rm GVO}(\vartheta)+\beta_{\rm KL}\mathcal{L}_{\rm KL}(\vartheta)\bigr], where ℒGVO\mathcal{L}_{\rm GVO} reinforces choices from searches with positive advantage AgA_{g} and βKL​ℒKL\beta_{\rm KL}\mathcal{L}_{\rm KL} regularizes divergence from the fixed post-warm-up actor (Appendix D). Using the PPO-style clipped objective (Schulman et al., 2017) for sampled choice yg,jy_{g,j} under context Hg,jH_{g,j} and legal support 𝒴g,j\mathcal{Y}_{g,j}, we have

ρg,j​(ϑ)=pϑ​(yg,j∣Hg,j,𝒴g,j)pϑk​(yg,j∣Hg,j,𝒴g,j),ℒGVO(ϑ)=−1G∑g=1G∑j=1Jgmin{ρg,j(ϑ)Ag,clip(ρg,j(ϑ),1−ϵc,1+ϵc)Ag},\begin{gathered}\rho_{g,j}(\vartheta)=\frac{p_{\vartheta}(y_{g,j}\mid H_{g,j},\mathcal{Y}_{g,j})}{p_{\vartheta_{k}}(y_{g,j}\mid H_{g,j},\mathcal{Y}_{g,j})},\\ \mathcal{L}_{\rm GVO}(\vartheta)=-\frac{1}{G}\!\sum_{g=1}^{G}\!\sum_{j=1}^{J_{g}}\!\min\bigl\{\rho_{g,j}(\vartheta)A_{g},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{g,j}(\vartheta),1-\epsilon_{c},1+\epsilon_{c})A_{g}\bigr\},\end{gathered} (14)

where jj indexes the JgJ_{g} sampled choices in search gg, ϑk=(θk,ψk)\vartheta_{k}=(\theta_{k},\psi_{k}) denotes the frozen collection parameters, and ρg,j\rho_{g,j} is the probability ratio between current and collection policies (evaluating Drafter probabilities for edit tokens and Policy probabilities for plan choices, with clip\operatorname{clip} radius ϵc∈(0,1)\epsilon_{c}\in(0,1) distinct from exploration rate ϵ\epsilon). Trajectory logs ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} record token contexts, legal supports, and behavior probabilities (which are empty for VERIFY steps) so that numerator and denominator are evaluated under identical contexts, supports, temperatures, masks, and exploration settings. During gradient computation, collection probabilities and advantages are held constant, invalid sampled edits retain their likelihood and cost, and each choice contributes once without search-length normalization. In the single exact-replay step of Alg. S3, ρg,j​(ϑk)=1\rho_{g,j}(\vartheta_{k})=1, so clipping is inactive and does not bound the update.

Finally, GVO freezes the updated improver Θk+1\Theta_{k+1} for the next collection round; because actor updates shift the continuation distribution, subsequent rounds collect fresh searches to recalibrate the Scorer under the fixed contract Γ\Gamma, with Drafter and Policy supervision based on complete-search returns (Appendix D).

4 Experimental Results

In this section, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation to demonstrate the efficacy of SpecRSI, centered on the following research questions (RQs):

  1. 1.

    RQ1: Does SpecRSI produce better successor agents? Section 4.2 compares SpecRSI against competitive baselines across tasks and backbones under matched evaluation settings.

  2. 2.

    RQ2: How do verification scope and planning in VATS affect search quality and cost? Section 4.3 examines verification scope, draft-ahead, and planning, with additional scorer and evidence-input controls in Appendix C.2.

  3. 3.

    RQ3: Does GVO learn a more effective improver? Section 4.4 compares frozen and GVO-updated improvers from identical starting agents and tracks cumulative gains over successive rounds.

  4. 4.

    RQ4: How do planning capacity and parallelism trade off gain, cost, and latency? Section 4.5 analyzes candidate-plan limits, full-lifecycle token expenditure, and multi-worker execution latency.

4.1 Evaluation Setup

Datasets. We evaluate five scientific tasks (PyBaMM (Sulzer et al., 2021), AQM (de Almeida et al., 2024), FDTD (Wu et al., 2024), Reactor (Braniff & Tian, 2024), and IRP (Violi et al., 2024))11 1 PyBaMM; ns-3. Our implementations: FDTD, Reactor, IRP. and four agent-system benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026), SWE-Pro (Deng et al., 2025), GPQA-hard100 (Rein et al., 2024), and AIME).22 2 Terminal-Bench 2.1; SWE-Pro; GPQA; AIME. We further evaluate specialized settings for code (SWE-Pro (Deng et al., 2025), HumanEval-Ext. (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP-Advanced (Austin et al., 2021), FixBench (Li et al., 2025)),33 3 SWE-Pro; HumanEval; MBPP; Fixbench-RTL. prompt (GPQA-hard100 (Rein et al., 2024), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), GSM8K-Opt. (Cobbe et al., 2021)),44 4 GPQA-hard100; MMLU-Pro; GSM8K-Opt. and workflow optimization (PlanBench (Valmeekam et al., 2023), Math (Fei et al., 2026), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), Game24 (Yao et al., 2023)).55 5 PlanBench; Math; MBPP; Game24. Here HumanEval-Ext., MBPP-Advanced, GPQA-hard100, and GSM8K-Opt. are benchmark-derived profiles, FixBench uses Fixbench-RTL, and workflow Math follows EMAS; where a benchmark appears in multiple settings, each experiment specifies its own cohort, starting agent, and verification contract.

Baselines. We benchmark SpecRSI against five groups of baselines: (1) scientific optimization, following Janus’s comparison protocols (Liu et al., 2026): Alg.-Only (AlphaEvolve-style program evolution with a fixed evaluator) (Novikov et al., 2025), Direct-LLM (LAEA-style candidate-quality prediction) (Hao et al., 2024), Embed-GP (a Gaussian-process surrogate on fixed code embeddings) (Snoek et al., 2012), and Janus; (2) system-level RSI (Tan et al., 2026): Initial, Data-RSI, Harness-RSI, Model-RSI, Fixed D→\toM→\toH, a failure-signature Static router, and MetaRSI-v1; (3) code optimization: DGM (Zhang et al., 2026a), SICA (Robeyns et al., 2025), HGM (Wang et al., 2026b), our non-learning Beam-Spec control with speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), and FlashEvolve (async/optional) (Hu et al., 2026); (4) prompt optimization: MIPROv2 (with/without demonstrations) (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024), Trace (Cheng et al., 2024), TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025), and GEPA/GEPA+Merge (Agrawal et al., 2026); and (5) workflow optimization: Genesis/Genesis+SOP (Fei et al., 2026), AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025), ADAS (Hu et al., 2025), and EMAS (Fei et al., 2026). All comparisons match edit permissions, where MetaRSI-H and SpecRSI-H restrict updates to D+H (prompts, tool workflows, and non-test data) with frozen model weights (Tan et al., 2026, Sec. 5.3), and SpecRSI executes direct checks. In cross-backbone transfer tests (Figure 4), we freeze the shared Qwen-trained improver across all ten scientific and twenty system backbones (nineteen beyond the reference model; see the online reproduction notes), matching starting agents, contracts, seeds, and evaluation caps (KK for Janus/SpecRSI in scientific tasks, and D+H splits and search caps for MetaRSI/SpecRSI in system tasks).

Evaluation Metrics. We report terminal gain (ΔK\Delta_{K}) and area under the budget curve (AUBC) on scientific tasks following Janus (Liu et al., 2026), alongside task scores and mean inference cost (CC). Token-accounted searches track initial and remaining budgets B0B_{0} and Bt≥0B_{t}\geq 0 (in k tokens) separately from the evaluation-call limit KK, which is fixed across scientific methods at K=140,130,160,135,120K=140,130,160,135,120 for PyBaMM, AQM, FDTD, Reactor, and IRP, respectively. Each call executes one instance’s full real-evaluation suite (counting failed runs, but excluding cached and proxy evaluations). Let sbs_{b} denote the held-out score of the complete admissible incumbent selected on validation after bb calls (with held-out scores never used during search selection), and let Δb=sb−s0\Delta_{b}=s_{b}-s_{0}. We compute

ΔK=sK−s0,AUBC=12​∑b=1K(Δb−1+Δb),C=∑i=1MTi103​M,\Delta_{K}=s_{K}-s_{0},\quad\mathrm{AUBC}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{b=1}^{K}(\Delta_{b-1}+\Delta_{b}),\quad C=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{M}T_{i}}{10^{3}M}, (15)

where MM is the number of evaluated instances and TiT_{i} sums all input and output inference tokens over instance ii’s full execution, including failed or unfinished attempts. Thus CC measures online inference cost in k tokens per task (whereas Figure 2A counts tokens up to the first qualifying outcome or termination, and seed totals or training-token costs are listed separately; Appendix C.1). Scientific gains use dimensionless task scores (Appendix B), and AUBC integrates gain over calls by carrying the final value forward to KK after early stopping. Task scores are reported as accuracy or success percentages (with absolute differences in percentage points, pp, and relative gains over the named baseline); higher gain, AUBC, and score and lower cost indicate better performance. Unless stated otherwise, we average three searches per training seed and report mean ±\pm SD across five seed means.

Implementation Details. We implement SpecRSI using Qwen3.5-35B-A3B66 6 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B as the reference backbone, equipping the Drafter with rank-16 LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) and using separate 256-dimensional branches for the Scorer and Policy. Supervised warm-up trains for one epoch using AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, followed by two reference GVO collection-and-update rounds with G=3G=3 independent complete searches per group (see Appendix B for full settings and Appendix C.2 for the 20-round extension).

4.2 Overall Performance (RQ1)

In this section, we benchmark SpecRSI across tasks and backbones.  Higher scientific gains. Across the five scientific tasks, SpecRSI improves mean terminal gain and call-axis AUBC over Janus by 60.0%–96.3% and 32.1%–91.6%, respectively (Table 1A).  Better system-level successors. Under matched D/H/M permissions, SpecRSI outperforms MetaRSI-v1 by 3.5–4.4 pp, while restricting updates to D+H retains a 3.48 pp average advantage (Table 1B).  Gains persist across backbones. Transferring the frozen improver across models improves all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs over Janus and outperforms MetaRSI-v1 by 1.30–2.70 pp across all twenty system backbones (Figure 4).

Benefits extend across optimization settings. On the eleven code, prompt, and workflow benchmarks, SpecRSI improves mean scores by 3.5–6.0 pp over the strongest baseline on each task while reducing inference cost by 3.2%–17.6% (Figure 5; see Appendix C.1 and Figure S1(A,B) for instance-level results).

4.3 VATS Ablations (RQ2)

In this section, we dissect verification scope and planning in VATS on PyBaMM (Figure 6).  Bundles improve accepted outcomes. With full-state inputs and draft-ahead disabled, bundled verification raises accepted gain from 4.8 to 6.3 pp and hit rate (the share of 125 searches returning a complete, admissible agent with positive gain) from 84% to 92%, while reducing search cost from 47.96 to 44.99 k tokens.  Draft-ahead and bundles yield the best mean outcomes. In the 2×22\times 2 factorial comparison, combining draft-ahead with bundled checks achieves the highest accepted gain (6.02 pp) and hit rate (92%) alongside the lowest cost (47.64 k tokens).  Planning improves the gain–cost trade-off. Full SpecRSI achieves the highest mean gain and lowest mean cost across all eight budget caps; at the 70% cap, it reaches 6.00 versus 4.73 pp for additive MILP planning while using 44.76 versus 49.29 k tokens (9.2% less). Under matched inputs, scoring continuation return (CR) also improves gain by 1.32 pp over candidate-quality scoring (CQ) at 7.4% lower search cost (Figure S2A,B; Appendix C.2).

4.4 Learning Effectiveness (RQ3)

In this section, we evaluate improver learning across starting agents and multi-round trajectories (Figure 7).  GVO updates improve search quality. When starting searches either from the original task agent or from the previous round’s output (without resetting the improver), GVO-only updates raise gains from 4.10/4.80 to 4.60/5.68 pp, respectively (Figure 7A). In the matched factorial comparison (Figure 7C), GVO adds 0.80 pp under Greedy search and 1.30 pp under VATS; overall, full SpecRSI outperforms Greedy with a frozen improver by 2.00 pp at 19.5% lower total token cost (including training).  Learning helps from the same starting agent. Holding the starting task agent fixed in a paired test, GVO updates increase gain from 5.7 to 6.9 pp (Figure 7A), yielding a paired improvement of 1.20 pp (95% CI [1.112,1.288][1.112,1.288], positive across all five seeds; Table S2).  Gains accumulate across rounds. Across 20 rounds (comparing frozen before-training improvers against after-training improvers updated each round via GVO or MetaRSI’s rule), cumulative gain reaches 42.1 pp for updated SpecRSI versus 29.6 pp for updated MetaRSI and 21.2 pp for frozen SpecRSI, with positive mean per-round gains throughout rounds 2–20 (Figure 7B; see also frozen-improver transfer in Figure 4B and Appendix C.2).

4.5 Resource Trade-offs (RQ4)

In this section, we examine candidate-plan limits, lifecycle costs, and parallel execution (Table 2).  More plans yield diminishing gains. Raising the candidate-plan limit from 8 to 32 increases gain from 5.2 to 6.3 pp, whereas doubling it to 64 adds only 0.2 pp while increasing planning cost from 3.9 to 5.6 k tokens (Table 2A).  SpecRSI uses fewer lifecycle tokens. SpecRSI achieves lower mean token usage across all seven lifecycle categories, reducing full-run expenditure (including training and serialized copies) from 112.7 k tokens for MetaRSI-v1 to 106.3 k tokens (−5.7%-5.7\%; Table 2B).  Parallel workers reduce latency but use more worker time. Scaling from one to eight concurrent workers cuts elapsed wall-clock time from 1,287 to 192 s (6.7×6.7\times) at the cost of 19.0% more total worker time, while twenty workers further reduce latency to 100 s (12.9×12.9\times) with 55.2% more worker time as mean gain rises from 6.3 to 6.7 pp (Table 2C).

5 Conclusion

In this work, we present SpecRSI, whose two-level loop extends incompletely evaluated parents but adopts only complete, admissible versions. VATS allocates edits and complementary checks by predicted verified continuation return; GVO updates the improver from completed searches under a fixed verification contract. SpecRSI improves terminal-gain and AUBC means over Janus in all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.30–2.70 pp in score across twenty backbones. Full planning outperforms six planning controls in mean held-out gain and mean total token cost across all eight budget caps. Starting-artifact controls support gains from improver updates beyond retaining stronger task agents. Instance-level comparisons show higher PyBaMM gain and SWE-Pro success with lower token cost. These results show that planning verification and learning the improver jointly improve agent performance and token efficiency.

Contents for Appendix

Appendix A Extended Related Work

Recursive self-improvement. Recent agent-optimization frameworks—including DGM, SICA, ADAS, AFlow, and GEPA—iteratively refine agent programs, workflows, or prompts (Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2026). To guide multi-step evolution, HGM expands lineages using descendant outcomes while scheduling evaluations separately (Wang et al., 2026b), Hyperagents directly modifies the meta-agent (Zhang et al., 2026b), MetaRSI adapts improvement operators and their scheduling (Tan et al., 2026), and Janus co-evolves target programs with screening proxies under real-validation gates (Liu et al., 2026). By contrast, SpecRSI learns both successor drafting and verification allocation directly from the net verified returns of complete searches.

Speculative decoding. Standard speculative decoding accelerates generation by verifying cheap draft tokens in parallel with a target model (Leviathan et al., 2023). In agentic settings, FlashEvolve asynchronously overlaps evolution stages (Hu et al., 2026). SpecRSI instead brings speculation to persistent agent revisions: only adopted versions require complete verification, whereas intermediate ancestors may remain partially evaluated.

Learning for agent improvement. Whereas GRPO estimates group-relative advantages across responses to the same prompt (Shao et al., 2024) and MAS2 trains meta-agents via Collaborative Tree Optimization (Wang et al., 2026a), GVO assigns credit across independent complete searches launched from matched starting states. Its search-level returns reward verified gains net of all incurred costs—including preparation as well as failed or unfinished branches—using realized suffix returns to train the Scorer and whole-search advantages to update the Drafter and Policy.

Appendix B Implementation Details

Appendix C More Experimental Results

In this section, we present instance-level RQ1 evaluations, additional RQ2–RQ3 controls, and qualitative case studies on PyBaMM and SWE-Pro, complementing Sections 4.2–4.4.

C.1 Instance-level Performance

In this subsection, we extend RQ1 to paired instances on PyBaMM and SWE-Pro (Figure S1) under the protocols in Table S3.  Higher gains accompany lower cost. SpecRSI improves PyBaMM terminal gain by 142.6% over Janus and SWE-Pro resolution rate by 6.0 pp over HGM, while reducing token expenditure by 7.0% and 9.2%, respectively.

C.2 Search and Learning Controls

In this subsection, we present additional VATS and GVO controls in Figure S2, with protocols detailed in Table S3.  Continuation targets and evidence improve search. Under matched inputs, continuation-return scoring (CR) improves gain by 1.32 pp (95% CI [1.184,1.456][1.184,1.456]) over complete-evaluation gain scoring (CQ) while using 3.52 k fewer tokens (7.4%), and full evidence yields 6.30 pp versus 3.20–5.80 pp under restricted inputs.  Supervision and GVO improve accepted gain. On identical plans, adding pairwise targets raises gain from 5.40 to 6.30 pp at higher training cost; relative to Greedy/frozen, VATS and GVO add 0.70 and 0.80 pp individually and 2.00 pp jointly (95% paired CI [0.452,3.548][0.452,3.548], interaction +0.50+0.50 pp, 95% CI [−0.520,1.520][-0.520,1.520]; Figure 7C).

C.3 Qualitative Case Studies

In this subsection, we present two representative cases in Tables S4 and S5, separating single-seed execution traces from five-seed summaries. Search costs count input/output and tool-return tokens, excluding simulator or test runtime and separately tracked LoRA training (the online supplement provides an additional D+H csvcut case with frozen model weights).

Appendix D Algorithms and Training

In this section, we state the execution, MILP, and training rules supplementing Section 3 and Algorithms S1–S3 (with hyperparameters in Appendix B).

KL regularization

Writing pg,jϑ=pϑ(⋅∣Hg,j,𝒴g,j)p_{g,j}^{\vartheta}=p_{\vartheta}(\cdot\mid H_{g,j},\mathcal{Y}_{g,j}), we define

ℒKL=1G​∑g=1G∑j=1Jg∑y∈𝒴g,jpg,jϑ​(y)​log⁡pg,jϑ​(y)pg,jϑ0​(y),\mathcal{L}_{\rm KL}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{g}}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{g,j}}p_{g,j}^{\vartheta}(y)\log\frac{p_{g,j}^{\vartheta}(y)}{p_{g,j}^{\vartheta_{0}}(y)}, (16)

where the post-warm-up reference ϑ0\vartheta_{0} remains fixed, detached, and strictly positive on the shared legal support, with both distributions evaluated under identical logged contexts, temperatures, masks, and exploration transforms.

Execution

Deployment runs a single frozen search, and forced continuations trigger no outer-loop updates. Disjoint preparation and execution ledgers charge all failed or unfinished work without imputing missing records as zero labels. At each step, the menu retains ACCEPT, feasible seeds, available edits, singleton checks, and affordable completions regardless of their isolated scores; every non-ACCEPT action consumes at least one attempt, leaving ACCEPT as the sole option when no other work is feasible, and inconsistent caps are rejected. Preparation tracks actual and reserved budget charges oB,o¯Bo_{B},\bar{o}_{B} alongside total expense and cap o,o¯o,\bar{o} (0≤oB≤o¯B≤B−0\leq o_{B}\leq\bar{o}_{B}\leq B^{-}); in Figure 6C, setting oB=o¯B=0o_{B}=\bar{o}_{B}=0 means BB caps drafting and verification while separately capped preparation enters total cost, with cache hits requiring matched state, scorer snapshot, and plan.

Completion MILP

Each job jj specifies covered keys KjK_{j}, reserved expense c¯j\bar{c}_{j}, attempts n¯j\bar{n}_{j}, and a setup group γ⁡(j)\gamma(j) with cost sγs_{\gamma}. Using binary decision variables xj,yγx_{j},y_{\gamma} for jobs and setups under target set K≠∅K\neq\varnothing and planning budget Bplan=B−−o¯BB_{\rm plan}=B^{-}-\bar{o}_{B}, the Solver solves

minxj,yγ∈{0,1}⁡C=∑jc¯j​xj+∑γsγ​yγ,∑j:ξ∈Kjxj≥1(ξ∈K),C≤Bplan,1≤∑jn¯jxj≤N,xj≤xi(i prerequisite of j),xi+xj≤1(i,j conflict),xj≤yγ⁡(j),yγ≤∑j:γ⁡(j)=γxj.\begin{gathered}\min_{x_{j},y_{\gamma}\in\{0,1\}}C=\sum_{j}\bar{c}_{j}x_{j}+\sum_{\gamma}s_{\gamma}y_{\gamma},\\ \sum_{j:\xi\in K_{j}}x_{j}\geq 1\ (\xi\in K),\quad C\leq B_{\rm plan},\quad 1\leq\sum_{j}\bar{n}_{j}x_{j}\leq N,\\ x_{j}\leq x_{i}\ (i\text{ prerequisite of }j),\quad x_{i}+x_{j}\leq 1\ (i,j\text{ conflict}),\\ x_{j}\leq y_{\gamma(j)},\qquad y_{\gamma}\leq\sum_{j:\gamma(j)=\gamma}x_{j}.\end{gathered} (17)

Only independently validated feasible covers seed the search (valid timeout incumbents need not be optimal); our implementation uses SciPy/HiGHS with round-robin targets and an independently seeded reservoir prior to observing outcomes.
